periods.activity_title: Body Turns: Feeling Full, Half, and Quarter

tasks_in_class.description: Keep turning around; freeze when teacher says 'Statue'. Notice how much you have turned from your original position.
Identify the child who made a full turn and the child who made a half turn. Give examples of real-life situations involving turns.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the idea of turning by asking children to stand, face the board, and then slowly spin on the spot. Ask: have you ever spun like a top, or watched a fan blade go round? These are all turns.

Let us play Statue, p.32 ("Keep turning around; freeze when teacher says 'Statue'..."). Children play in open space or at their desks. Teacher calls 'Statue' at different moments so some children have completed a full circle, some a half, some a quarter. After each freeze, pairs compare their ending positions.

Discuss, p.32 ("Identify the child who made a full turn and the child..."). Whole-class discussion: which child looks the same way as at the start? Which now faces behind? Draw a simple circle on the board and mark full, half, and quarter arcs with arrows to record what the class decides.

Quick round: teacher calls a direction (full, half, quarter) and children mime the matching turn. Then each child shares one real-life example of a turn from their own experience: clock hands, a door, a spinning top.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often conflate the amount turned with the final position — a child who ends up facing backwards has made a half turn, not 'the back turn'. Anchor each freeze moment to where the child started by marking a sticky-note arrow on the floor or desk edge. This concrete reference point is the seed for everything the chapter builds next.
materials: Open floor space or cleared desks
Sticky-note arrows or chalk marks for start positions

periods.activity_title: Two Halves Make a Whole: Objects That Turn

tasks_in_class.description: Complete: 2 half turns = ___ turn; 2 quarter turns = ___ turn; 4 quarter turns = ___ turn.
Hold green straw steady; turn yellow straw. Observe different turns of the yellow straw using Pragya's straw-and-paper-clip model.
For each object (clothes clip, door with hinge, tongs, scissors, file cover) tick the maximum possible turn: less than 1/4, exactly 1/4, or more than 1/4.

time_bands.activity: Fill in, p.33 ("Complete: 2 half turns = ___ turn; 2 quarter turns = ___ turn..."). Children perform the combinations using their own body first — stand, do two half-turns, notice they are back to start. Record the completed statements on the board and invite children to explain their reasoning aloud.

Observe, p.33 ("Hold green straw steady; turn yellow straw..."). Each pair makes a quick straw-and-paper-clip model using two straws and a clip. One partner holds the green straw flat on the desk; the other turns the yellow straw to show a full, then half, then quarter turn. Pairs then try to make a turn that seems to be between a quarter and a half.

Check and tick table, p.33 ("For each object — clothes clip, door with hinge, tongs, scissors, file cover — tick the maximum possible turn..."). Teacher brings or mimes one object; children use their straw model to estimate before ticking. Groups share and justify disagreements.

Closing discussion: children name one more everyday object and the class decides together whether its maximum turn is less than, equal to, or more than a quarter. Teacher records responses on the board as a brief class list.

periods.teacher_notes: Children commonly tick 'exactly 1/4' for scissors because the blades cross at what looks like a right-angle corner, but the question asks about the maximum possible turn of the object as a whole. Invite children to open scissors as far as they go and compare against the straw model held at a quarter-turn position. Additional practice for classifying objects is available at Write, p.33 and Check and tick bullets, p.33.
materials: Two drinking straws and one paper clip per pair
Objects or pictures: clothes clip, door hinge, tongs, scissors, file cover

periods.activity_title: Paper Fan Angles: Naming What We See

tasks_in_class.description: Make a paper fan by folding rectangular paper every 2 cm and pasting ice cream sticks. Use the fan to show different acute and obtuse angles.
Look at angles A–H marked on the notebook-cover house. Write whether each is right, acute, or obtuse.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q(a), p.34 ("Make a paper fan by folding rectangular paper every 2 cm and pasting ice cream sticks..."). Children fold an A4 strip accordion-style and attach two ice cream sticks. Teacher demonstrates on the board how spreading the fan a tiny bit gives an acute angle, spreading to a right angle (linking back to the quarter-turn idea from the body-turning work), and spreading further gives an obtuse angle, while fully flat gives a straight angle.

Let Us Do Q(b), p.35 ("Look at angles A–H marked on the notebook-cover house. Write whether each is right, acute, or obtuse."). Children hold their fan beside each labelled angle in the book to compare. Teacher circulates and asks: 'Is your fan opening smaller or bigger than a quarter turn here?' Children record their answers and pairs cross-check.

Whole-class debrief: teacher draws a summary table on the board matching turn-fraction to angle name (less than quarter → acute; quarter → right; between quarter and half → obtuse; half → straight). Children call out their answers for each labelled angle and reach consensus.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error is calling a large obtuse angle 'straight' because it looks wide; the fan makes the boundary visible — a straight angle means the two sticks lie in one line. The paper fan connects naturally to the body-turning and straw-model work by making the 'opening' of the angle a physical act children can control. Additional notebook tasks for this section are Let Us Do Q(c) and the acute-turns question on p.35, which can be assigned as additional practice.
materials: Two ice cream sticks per child

periods.activity_title: Reasoning About Acute Turns and Angle Combinations

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do acute-turns question, p.35
tasks_in_class.description: Make an acute turn with straws or fan, then make another acute turn. Determine whether the two acute turns together can form another acute turn.
Make a 5-sided shape with 2 right angles, 2 obtuse angles, and 1 acute angle in your notebook.

time_bands.activity: Teacher places the fan from the previous unit of work on the desk and invites a child to open it to a tiny acute angle. Class confirms it is acute. Teacher poses the question: if we make two such turns one after another, must the result also be acute, or might it be something else?

Let Us Do acute-turns question, p.35 ("Make an acute turn with straws or fan, then make another acute turn. Determine whether the two acute turns together can form another acute turn."). Children work in pairs using straws or fans. They try small + small (e.g., 1/16 + 1/16) and larger + larger (e.g., nearly a quarter + nearly a quarter). Pairs record: 'Our two acute turns together made a ___ angle.' Teacher draws a few examples on the board, showing that the total can remain acute, become right, or become obtuse.

Let Us Do Q(c), p.35 ("Make a 5-sided shape with 2 right angles, 2 obtuse angles, and 1 acute angle in your notebook."). Children draw freely and then label each angle using the fan to confirm type. Partners check each other's drawings.

Brief share: one or two children hold up their 5-sided shapes and the class names the angles together. Teacher summarises that angle type depends entirely on the size of the opening, not on where the shape sits or how it looks overall.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often assume that two acute angles must always give an acute result; letting them discover through the straw or fan that two large-acute turns can sum to an obtuse or right angle is the key insight of this unit. The 5-sided shape task reveals whether children can deliberately produce an angle of a chosen type, which is a stronger test than merely naming given angles.
materials: Paper fans from the previous making activity (or fresh strips)

periods.activity_title: Folding Circles into Eighths: Building a Measuring Tool

tasks_in_class.description: Cut a circle from tracing paper, fold into 8 equal parts, attach straw at centre, mark starting point.

Show 1/8, 2/8, 1/4, 3/8 turns of the straw. Identify angle type for 2/8 and 4/8 turns. Continue to 5/8, 6/8, 7/8, 8/8; check when 3/4 and full turn are complete. Cut 1/8 and 2/8 parts and paste on card as measuring tools.

time_bands.activity: Angle Measuring Tool Q(a), p.36 ("Cut a circle from tracing paper, fold into 8 equal parts, attach straw at centre, mark starting point."). Teacher demonstrates folding in half, then half again, then half again, to produce 8 equal sectors. Children follow along. The straw is attached with a pin or tape at the centre.

Angle Measuring Tool Q(b), p.36 ("Show 1/8, 2/8, 1/4, 3/8 turns of the straw. Identify angle type for 2/8 and 4/8 turns. Continue to 5/8, 6/8, 7/8, 8/8..."). Children rotate the straw sector by sector and record: which turn gives a right angle? Which give acute? Obtuse? Class builds a shared table on the board. Children then cut the 1/8 and 2/8 sectors and paste them on stiff card.

Quick verification: teacher holds up a corner of a notebook and asks children to use their 2/8 card to confirm it is a right angle. Then teacher shows a slightly open book and asks: is this more or less than 2/8?

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes fold unevenly so that their eighths are not equal; before cutting, ask them to hold the folded circle to the light and check that all fold lines pass through one central point. Connecting 2/8 = 1/4 = right angle links fraction equivalence (developed in the combining-turns work) to the new measuring tool.
materials: Stiff card or cardboard for pasting sectors

section_titles: Angle Measuring Tool — Sixths and Twelfths
periods.activity_title: Folding into Sixths and Twelfths: Finer Measures

tasks_in_class.description: Cut a circle from tracing paper; fold in half then into 3 equal parts. Attach straw, mark starting point; show turns of 1/6, 2/6, … full circle. Cut 1/6 and 2/6 parts; fold 1/6 in half to make 1/12. Paste on card as measuring tools.
In circles showing endpoints of 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 turns, draw arrows to show the starting points.

time_bands.activity: Angle Measuring Tool sixths, p.37 ("Cut a circle from tracing paper; fold in half then into 3 equal parts. Attach straw, mark starting point; show turns of 1/6, 2/6, … full circle. Cut 1/6 and 2/6 parts; fold 1/6 in half to make 1/12. Paste on card as measuring tools."). Teacher models folding a circle in half and then folding that half into three equal parts by bringing one edge to the midpoint. Children make their own sixths circle. They add the 1/6 and 2/6 card sectors to their collection from the eighths unit.

Let Us Think Q1, p.37 ("In circles showing endpoints of 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 turns, draw arrows to show the starting points."). Children reason backwards: if the straw ended here after a quarter turn, where must it have begun? They use their card measuring tools to check by placing and rotating. Pairs discuss and compare drawings.

Teacher draws two quick circles on the board — one with an endpoint marked for a 1/6 turn, one for a 3/6 turn — and asks children to call out or draw where the starting point must be. Connects to the idea that the same angle can be reached from many starting points.

periods.teacher_notes: The trickiest fold is the thirds division; demonstrate by folding the semicircle and adjusting until both thirds look equal, then crease firmly. The reverse-arrow task in Let Us Think Q1 is a genuine spatial reasoning challenge — children who struggle can place their card sector on the printed endpoint and rotate until one edge aligns, then trace the other edge as the starting arrow.
materials: Stiff card sectors from the eighths unit

periods.activity_title: Guess, Measure, and Name: Using the Tool on Angles

tasks_in_class.description: Guess the measure of each angle shown; then check using the angle-measuring tool (use combinations). State whether each is acute, right, or obtuse.
Guess the measure of turns made by the arrow in cases (a)–(d). Verify using combinations of angle-measuring tools.
Measure each angle in the given shapes (a), (b), (c). Write measures in terms of turns; describe each as acute, obtuse, or right.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q1, p.38 ("Guess the measure of each angle shown; then check using the angle-measuring tool (use combinations)..."). Children first write a guess in pencil, then place their card sectors. Teacher models one example: lay the 1/8 card, see if the angle is smaller or larger, add or remove a sector. Children record type alongside measure.

Let Us Do Q2, p.38 ("Guess the measure of turns made by the arrow in cases (a)–(d). Verify using combinations of angle-measuring tools."). Children work individually, then compare guesses with a partner before measuring. Pairs whose guesses differ discuss why before checking.

Let Us Do Q3, p.38 ("Measure each angle in the given shapes (a), (b), (c). Write measures in terms of turns; describe each as acute, obtuse, or right."). Children work through all three shapes. Teacher circulates asking: 'How did you know to use two sectors here?'
Quick class share: teacher asks which shape had the most right angles and which had the largest obtuse angle. Children respond verbally.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes place a sector card with the wrong edge as the baseline; remind them that one straight edge of the sector must lie exactly along one arm of the angle being measured. The estimate-then-verify sequence in Q1 and Q2 builds the estimation habit that is central to this chapter's measurement strand.
materials: Card sector measuring tools from units 5 and 6 (1/8, 2/8, 1/6, 2/6, 1/12)

periods.activity_title: Drawing Turns: Fractions on the Page

tasks_in_class.description: Draw angles for given measures of turns (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/12, 1/4) using the given lines.
Draw the angles formed by: 1/2, 1/4, 2/4, 1/6, 4/6, 3/12, 1/2+1/4, and 1/8+1/6 turns in your notebook.

homework.description: Find the turn made by the minute hand for each time interval [(a) 15 min, (b) 30 min, (c) 45 min, (d) 1/12 full turn → ? min, (e) full turn → ? min, (f) 1/6 full turn → ? min, (g) 4/12 full turn → ? min]; draw final clock positions.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q4, p.39 ("Draw angles for given measures of turns — 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/12, 1/4 — using the given lines."). Children use their card sectors to position the second arm of each angle. Teacher demonstrates Q4's first item on the board: place 2/8 card along the given line, mark where the sector edge falls, draw the arm. Children continue independently.

Let Us Do Q5, p.39 ("Draw the angles formed by: 1/2, 1/4, 2/4, 1/6, 4/6, 3/12, 1/2+1/4, and 1/8+1/6 turns in your notebook."). Children draw a starting line, place and combine sectors, and draw the second arm. For the combination turns (1/2+1/4, 1/8+1/6), children first estimate the result type before measuring.
Pairs exchange notebooks and check: does their partner's 1/4 turn look like a right angle? Does 1/2+1/4 look like a three-quarter turn? Brief verbal confirmations around the class.

periods.teacher_notes: A common difficulty in Q5 is combining unlike-denominator turns (1/8+1/6) without converting; children can simply place the 1/8 sector and then the 1/6 sector edge-to-edge and draw the total opening directly — no fraction arithmetic is needed at this stage. Q6 on p.39 (minute-hand turns) is set as an unhurried homework task because it requires children to connect clock time to turns, which works well when children can observe a real clock at home.

periods.activity_title: Which Way Did It Turn? Clockwise and Anti-clockwise

tasks_in_class.description: Observe direction while opening a tap, unscrewing a lid, and loosening a nut. Determine whether each moves clockwise or anti-clockwise.
For each of the four creature pairs making a quarter turn, tick whether the movement is clockwise or anti-clockwise.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a clock face on the board and traces the hands moving clockwise. Then traces anti-clockwise. Children mime both directions with an arm extended. Teacher introduces the vocabulary: clockwise follows the clock-hand direction; anti-clockwise is the opposite.

Try these, p.40 ("Observe direction while opening a tap, unscrewing a lid, and loosening a nut. Determine whether each moves clockwise or anti-clockwise."). Children mime opening a tap and an imaginary jar lid at their desks, then decide and show by rotating a fist in the right direction. Class reaches consensus on each action and records answers.

Tick direction, p.40 ("For each of the four creature pairs making a quarter turn, tick whether the movement is clockwise or anti-clockwise."). Children work independently in the book. Teacher draws the four creature pictures on the board with arrows; class discusses any disagreements by tracing the arrow relative to the clock-face reference.

Closing challenge: teacher stands and makes a quarter turn. Children write 'CW' or 'ACW' on their slates or paper. Then children take turns calling a direction (clockwise or anti-clockwise) and their partner mimes the corresponding quarter turn.

periods.teacher_notes: Direction of turn is often confused with starting or ending position; use the clock-face drawn on the board as a persistent reference so children can always compare. A reliable check is to ask: 'If the top of the creature's head follows a clock hand, does it go right-and-down (clockwise) or left-and-down (anti-clockwise)?'
materials: Blackboard with a clock face drawn
Slates or small whiteboards for quick responses

tasks_in_class.description: Complete the table: given starting direction and turns (e.g., 'North, two right angles clockwise'), fill in the ending direction for all 7 rows.
Padma faces the toy shop. Determine what place she faces after a half turn clockwise. Find another way she can turn to face the same place.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a compass rose (N, S, E, W) on the board. A volunteer stands in the centre of the room facing the board (North). Teacher calls: 'Make one right-angle turn clockwise' — child turns to face East. Class sees how the compass rose maps to the child's body.

Fun with Turns Q1, p.41 ("Complete the table: given starting direction and turns, fill in the ending direction for all 7 rows."). Children work individually. For each row, they may stand and mime the turns if it helps. Teacher circulates; for any row where answers differ, the class debates using the compass rose on the board.

Fun with Turns Q2, p.41 ("Padma faces the toy shop. Determine what place she faces after a half turn clockwise. Find another way she can turn to face the same place."). Children solve the first question, then work in pairs to find the alternative turning route. Pairs share their alternative and the class checks whether both routes truly land on the same facing.

Brief reflection: teacher asks — 'Can a clockwise turn and an anti-clockwise turn ever bring you to the same facing? When?' Children share ideas; teacher records one or two examples on the board without resolving the question fully, leaving space for the synthesis unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often lose track of cumulative turns when a row in Q1 has two or three steps; encourage them to draw a small compass rose and mark their current facing after each step. Fun with Turns Q2's alternative-route question is the first time the chapter explicitly asks for a different path to the same answer, which is the core of spatial reasoning in this context.
materials: Notebooks and pencils for working out turns

section_titles: Angle Measuring Tool — Sixths and Twelfths
periods.activity_title: The Great Turn Challenge: Connecting Every Idea

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents a single opening prompt on the board: 'A minute hand starts at 12 and moves clockwise for 15 minutes. What type of angle has it traced? What fraction of a full turn is that? Is the turn clockwise or anti-clockwise?' Children write individual responses, drawing on the full range of concepts from the chapter.

Gallery of turns: each child folds a fresh strip of paper into a fan and opens it to show one named angle — the teacher calls out 'Show me an obtuse angle', 'Show me 3/8 of a full turn', 'Show me a straight angle'. Children hold up fans; the class checks for agreement. Teacher uses the compass rose on the board to connect: 'A 1/4 clockwise turn from North lands you at East — which angle type did you just make?'

Synthesis puzzle in pairs: Teacher writes on the board — 'Riya faces West. She makes two clockwise right-angle turns. Where does she face? What total fraction of a full turn did she make? Draw the two turns using a starting line in your notebook.' Pairs work together, combining the compass-direction reasoning with the angle-measuring-tool ideas. Pairs share and compare drawings.

Quick-fire connections round: teacher poses rapid questions drawing on all chapter strands — 'Name one object that makes more than a quarter turn but less than a half turn. Is 3/6 of a full turn the same as a half turn? What angle does a 1/8 turn make?' Children respond with hand signals or brief written answers.

Closing reflection: each child writes one sentence — 'An angle is …' — completing the definition in their own words, drawing on body turns, fraction language, angle names, and direction vocabulary from across the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit weaves together every strand: the body-turn origin of angle, the fraction language of measuring tools, the naming of angle types, clockwise and anti-clockwise direction, and compass reasoning. The synthesis puzzle is designed so that children who are strong on fractions but shaky on compass directions must lean on their partner and vice versa — a deliberate collaboration opportunity.
materials: A4 paper strips for fans (one per child)

items.prompt: Priya stands facing the window. She turns around and now faces the door, which is exactly behind her. What kind of turn did Priya make?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A half turn. Priya now faces exactly the opposite direction, which is what a half turn produces.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A half turn brings you to face the opposite direction from where you started.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be thinking of a quarter turn as any change of facing, without connecting it to facing a direction at 90 degrees from the start.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses a full turn (returning to the original facing) with any large movement.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may not recognise that facing a different direction requires a turn to have been made.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student stand and physically turn to face behind; stretch: ask what turn would bring Priya back to face the window again.

exercise.description: Keep turning around; freeze when teacher says 'Statue'. Notice how much you have turned from your original position.

items.prompt: Hold one arm straight out in front of you. This is your starting position. Turn your arm to the side until it points directly to your right. What kind of turn did your arm make? Name one everyday object that can make this same kind of turn.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The arm made a quarter turn. Accept any object whose maximum turn is exactly a quarter, such as a door with a hinge or a tap handle (if it stops at a right angle).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Arm extended forward to pointing directly sideways covers exactly one quarter of a full circle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a straw-and-paper-clip model to show the arm movement; stretch: ask them to show a different object and describe whether its maximum turn is more or less than a quarter.

exercise.description: Hold green straw steady; turn yellow straw. Observe different turns of the yellow straw using Pragya's straw-and-paper-clip model.

items.prompt: Open your notebook so that the front cover and the back are fully flat on the desk — the cover makes a straight line with the back. What angle name do we give to the opening the cover has made? Now close the notebook partway so the opening is smaller than a right angle. What is this angle called?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The fully flat cover makes a straight angle (half turn). The smaller opening is an acute angle (less than a quarter turn).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A half turn produces a straight angle; an opening smaller than a quarter turn produces an acute angle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a paper fan to match each position and read off the angle name; stretch: ask what angle is formed when the cover is opened exactly to a right angle and how many turns that is.

exercise.description: Make a paper fan by folding rectangular paper every 2 cm and pasting ice cream sticks. Use the fan to show different acute and obtuse angles.

items.prompt: A circle is folded equally into 8 parts and a straw is attached at the centre. The straw is turned 4 sectors from the starting line. What does this turn equal?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A half turn. 4 sectors out of 8 equal parts is 4/8, which equals 1/2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: 4 out of 8 equal sectors = 4/8 = 1/2 of a full turn.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may associate '4' with a quarter without computing the fraction of the whole.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may think that reaching the halfway point means completing a full circle.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be counting the remaining 4 sectors rather than the sectors already turned.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student fold a paper strip into 8 equal parts and fold 4 of them over to see the fraction physically; stretch: ask which number of sectors would give a three-quarter turn.

exercise.description: Cut a circle from tracing paper, fold into 8 equal parts, attach straw at centre, mark starting point.

items.section_title: Angle Measuring Tool — Sixths and Twelfths
items.prompt: A circle is divided into 6 equal parts. One of the 1/6 sectors is folded exactly in half. What fraction of a full turn does this folded piece show?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1/12. Folding a 1/6 sector in half produces a piece that is half of 1/6, which equals 1/12 of the full circle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Half of 1/6 = 1/12 of a full circle.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student did not apply the fold and still reads the original sector size.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be confusing the sixths tool with the eighths tool.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have doubled instead of halved the sector.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically fold a 1/6 card sector in half and compare its size against the 1/12 marked on the circle; stretch: ask how many 1/12 sectors make a half turn.

exercise.description: Cut a circle from tracing paper; fold in half then into 3 equal parts. Attach straw, mark starting point; show turns of 1/6, 2/6, … full circle. Cut 1/6 and 2/6 parts; fold 1/6 in half to make 1/12. Paste on card as measuring tools.

items.prompt: Rohan opens a tap by turning the handle. The handle moves from the top position towards the left side, going down and round. In which direction is the handle turning?

options.label: B
options.text: Both clockwise and anti-clockwise at the same time

options.label: D
options.text: No direction, because taps do not turn

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Anti-clockwise. The handle moves from top toward the left, which is the direction opposite to clock hands.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Top moving to the left means the handle follows the direction opposite to clock hands — anti-clockwise.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have confused the direction by imagining looking at the tap from behind or from underneath.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student does not understand that a single turn has one direction at a time.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not connected the physical action of opening a tap to the concept of turning.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to mime opening a tap and observe which way their fist turns relative to a clock face drawn on the board; stretch: ask which direction they would turn the tap to close it and why.

exercise.description: Observe direction while opening a tap, unscrewing a lid, and loosening a nut. Determine whether each moves clockwise or anti-clockwise.

items.prompt: Kavya spins in a circle and stops back at her starting position. Dev spins the same way but stops when he is exactly facing behind him. Who has turned more — Kavya or Dev? Explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Kavya has turned more. She made a full turn (a complete circle) while Dev made only a half turn (ending up facing behind him, which is half of a full circle).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the fraction of a full circle each person completed: full turn > half turn.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: encourage the student to stand and mime both turns before writing; stretch: ask how many of Dev's turns would equal one of Kavya's turns.

exercise.description: Identify the child who made a full turn and the child who made a half turn. Give examples of real-life situations involving turns.

items.prompt: A door opens to its widest position and makes exactly 2 quarter turns from fully closed. How many quarter turns is that in total? What is this equal to in half turns? Write a number sentence to show your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2 quarter turns in total. 2 quarter turns = 1 half turn. Number sentence: 2 quarter turns = 1 half turn.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Two quarter turns combine to make one half turn because 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student demonstrate with a straw model, making one quarter turn then another, and count the halves; stretch: ask how many quarter turns are needed to make a full turn and write the number sentence.

exercise.description: Complete: 2 half turns = ___ turn; 2 quarter turns = ___ turn; 4 quarter turns = ___ turn.

items.prompt: Tongs are opened as wide as they can go. Which of the following best describes the maximum turn the tongs can make?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: More than a quarter turn. Tongs open well beyond a right angle when fully spread.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the maximum opening of the tongs to the right-angle (quarter-turn) position to judge which category it falls in.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be thinking of the closed or nearly closed position of the tongs rather than the maximum.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be confusing the look of the crossed handles with a right angle.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has overgeneralised — tongs cannot make a complete revolution.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mime opening tongs and use a paper fan held at the quarter-turn position as a reference; stretch: ask the student to estimate whether the maximum tong opening is closer to a half turn or a quarter turn.

exercise.description: For each object (clothes clip, door with hinge, tongs, scissors, file cover) tick the maximum possible turn: less than 1/4, exactly 1/4, or more than 1/4.

items.prompt: A clock shows 3 o'clock. The hour hand moves to 6 o'clock. What type of angle has the hour hand traced from 3 to 6? Explain why using the idea of turns.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The hour hand traces a right angle. Moving from 3 to 6 is a quarter of the full clock face, which is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn produces a right angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A quarter turn = right angle; from 3 to 6 on a clock is one quarter of the full circle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a clock face and mark the arc from 3 to 6, then compare it to the quarter-turn position on a paper fan; stretch: ask what angle is traced if the hand continues from 6 to 9 and whether the total from 3 to 9 is acute, right, or obtuse.

exercise.description: Look at angles A–H marked on the notebook-cover house. Write whether each is right, acute, or obtuse.

items.prompt: Arjun opens a book a little bit (a very small opening) and calls it an acute angle. His friend Meera opens her book a lot more — bigger than a right angle but not fully flat. What is the name of Meera's angle? If Arjun adds his angle to Meera's angle, is the combined angle definitely bigger than a straight angle? Explain your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Meera's angle is obtuse. The combined angle is not definitely bigger than a straight angle — it depends on the actual sizes. A tiny acute added to a small obtuse could still be less than a straight angle; only if the obtuse is very large (close to a straight angle) and the acute is not tiny would the sum exceed a straight angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Acute + obtuse can sum to less than, equal to, or greater than a straight angle depending on the actual sizes of each angle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: pair-share — one child uses the fan for Arjun's angle and another for Meera's, then combine the fans and compare to the half-turn (straight) position; stretch: ask the student to find a combination of acute and obtuse that gives exactly a straight angle.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do acute-turns question, p.35
exercise.description: Make an acute turn with straws or fan, then make another acute turn. Determine whether the two acute turns together can form another acute turn.

items.prompt: A student uses a folded-circle tool with 8 equal sectors to measure an angle. She finds the angle is bigger than 2/8 but smaller than 3/8. Which type of angle is it?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Obtuse angle. The angle is larger than 2/8 (which is a right angle = 1/4 turn) but smaller than 3/8 (which is less than a half turn), so it lies in the obtuse range.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Angles greater than a right angle (2/8) but less than a straight angle (4/8) are obtuse.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may know that 2/8 = right angle but not recognise that the given angle is larger than 2/8.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may not have compared 2/8 to the boundary values and placed the angle below the right-angle threshold.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have confused 3/8 with 4/8 (the straight angle threshold).

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student place 2/8 and 3/8 sectors on the paper and see the range the angle falls in; stretch: ask the student to state the exact fraction range (as eighths) for all four angle types.

exercise.description: Guess the measure of each angle shown; then check using the angle-measuring tool (use combinations). State whether each is acute, right, or obtuse.

items.section_title: Angle Measuring Tool — Sixths and Twelfths
items.prompt: A circle has an arrow pointing to the right (the 3 o'clock position). This is the end point of a 1/4 turn. Draw where the arrow started.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The starting arrow points straight up (the 12 o'clock position). A 1/4 turn clockwise from 12 o'clock ends at 3 o'clock.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Work backwards from the endpoint: subtract one quarter turn to find the starting position.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a 2/8 card sector to place the endpoint and rotate backwards to find the start; stretch: ask where the starting arrow would be if the same endpoint was reached by a 1/2 turn instead.

exercise.description: In circles showing endpoints of 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 turns, draw arrows to show the starting points.

items.prompt: A ladybird sits on a leaf facing North. It makes a quarter turn so it now faces East. Which direction did it turn?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Clockwise. Turning from North to East is a quarter turn in the same direction as clock hands move.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: On a compass rose, moving from North to East is the same direction as clock hands — clockwise.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have reversed the direction, perhaps confusing North-to-East with left-to-right movement.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student does not understand that a single quarter turn can only be in one direction.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not connect a change of facing from North to East with the act of turning.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a compass rose on the board; have the student trace North to East and compare to the clock-hand direction; stretch: ask which direction the ladybird would turn to go from East back to North in the shorter route.

exercise.description: For each of the four creature pairs making a quarter turn, tick whether the movement is clockwise or anti-clockwise.

items.prompt: Sania stands facing South. She makes two right-angle turns clockwise. Which direction does she face now? Show your working step by step.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sania faces North. Step 1: South + one right-angle clockwise = West. Step 2: West + one right-angle clockwise = North.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Track each quarter-turn clockwise on the compass rose: South → West → North.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a compass rose and mark each step with an arrow; stretch: ask the student to find a different combination of turns (including anti-clockwise) that also ends at North starting from South.

exercise.description: Complete the table: given starting direction and turns (e.g., 'North, two right angles clockwise'), fill in the ending direction for all 7 rows.

items.prompt: Ramu faces East. He wants to face West. He can do it with one half turn. Write one other way Ramu can face West using only right-angle turns. State the number of turns and their direction.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Accept any correct combination, for example: two right-angle turns clockwise (East → South → West), or two right-angle turns anti-clockwise (East → North → West).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Two quarter turns in the same direction equal a half turn and change facing to the opposite direction.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student stand, face East (or a chosen wall), and physically try right-angle turns to find a route to West; stretch: ask whether there is a way using three right-angle turns and justify the answer.

exercise.description: Padma faces the toy shop. Determine what place she faces after a half turn clockwise. Find another way she can turn to face the same place.

items.prompt: A straight horizontal line is drawn on your page. Using the line as one arm, draw the angle formed by a 3/8 turn. Label the angle with its measure (3/8 turn) and write whether it is acute, right, or obtuse.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The second arm should be drawn so that it opens 3/8 of a full circle from the given line (between a right angle and a straight angle). Label: 3/8 turn. Type: obtuse (since 3/8 is more than 2/8 = right angle, and less than 4/8 = straight angle).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the 3/8 card sector along the baseline, mark the far edge, draw the arm — 3/8 is between 2/8 and 4/8, so obtuse.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a pre-drawn baseline and let the student place the card sectors to find the arm position before drawing; stretch: draw a second angle for 5/8 of a turn and name it.

exercise.description: Draw angles for given measures of turns (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/12, 1/4) using the given lines.

items.prompt: The minute hand of a clock starts at 12. It moves clockwise for 20 minutes. (a) What fraction of a full turn has it made? (b) How many minutes does the minute hand take to complete a full turn?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) 20 minutes is one-third of 60 minutes, so the minute hand makes 1/3 of a full turn, equivalently 2/6 of a full turn. (b) The minute hand completes a full turn in 60 minutes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the given minutes by 60 to find the fraction of the full turn; a full turn takes 60 minutes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a clock face, mark 12 and 4 (the 20-minute position), and let the student count the spaces out of 12; stretch: ask what fraction of a full turn is made in 45 minutes and draw the final clock position.

exercise.description: Find the turn made by the minute hand for each time interval [(a) 15 min, (b) 30 min, (c) 45 min, (d) 1/12 full turn → ? min, (e) full turn → ? min, (f) 1/6 full turn → ? min, (g) 4/12 full turn → ? min]; draw final clock positions.
